stem: Shortly after extubation, a client develops new inspiratory stridor, increasing work of breathing, and a falling oxygen saturation. Which nursing response is most appropriate?

options.A: Assume laryngospasm is the diagnosis and wait for spontaneous resolution before reassessing the airway
options.B: Treat the finding as possible upper-airway obstruction: immediately assess and support oxygenation/ventilation, summon airway-qualified assistance, and prepare for escalation such as reintubation if obstruction is significant
options.C: Offer oral fluids to soothe airway irritation and reassess after the client has swallowed
options.D: Transfer the client from the recovery area because post-extubation stridor is an expected finding after general anesthesia

rationale: Post-extubation stridor indicates clinically important upper-airway narrowing and is not specific for laryngospasm. Post-intubation laryngeal edema is a common cause, while laryngospasm, angioedema/anaphylaxis, foreign body, hematoma, and vocal-cord problems are among the differential diagnoses. With increasing work of breathing and falling oxygen saturation, the priority is immediate airway and oxygenation/ventilation support with rapid escalation to airway-qualified personnel; prompt reintubation may be required when significant obstruction is suspected. Oral intake and transfer are unsafe during active airway compromise, and diagnostic labeling should not delay stabilization.
educational_objective: New post-extubation stridor with respiratory deterioration is an airway emergency cue; prioritize airway/oxygenation support and rapid escalation rather than assuming a single diagnosis.
source_version_date: Extubation last updated 2023-02-09; Post-Intubation Laryngeal Edema last updated 2023-07-04; current NCBI Bookshelf content verified 2026-08-17
source_locator: Extubation — Management of Post-extubation Stridor: oxygen/CPAP options when stable and prompt reintubation if significant airway obstruction is suspected. Post-Intubation Laryngeal Edema — Differential Diagnosis and Consultations: laryngeal edema as common cause of post-extubation stridor; differentiate from laryngospasm, angioedema/anaphylaxis, foreign body, hematoma, vocal-cord palsy.
source_claim_supported: Post-extubation stridor can reflect laryngeal edema or other upper-airway causes and significant obstruction may require prompt reintubation; the clinical priority is airway/oxygenation management rather than diagnosing laryngospasm from stridor alone.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential — Therapeutic Procedures, printed p. 44 (PDF page 47): assess client response to recovery from local, regional or general anesthesia; monitor before/after procedures; recognize changes and intervene as needed
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — postanesthesia airway complication assessment
correction_summary: Rejected the source's forced diagnosis of laryngospasm because post-extubation stridor has multiple defensible causes, especially laryngeal edema. Rebuilt the item around urgent airway assessment/support and escalation, and corrected the blueprint from Physiological Adaptation to Reduction of Risk Potential.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: Current NCBI Extubation and Post-Intubation Laryngeal Edema chapters reviewed; management and differential sections directly verified.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: Stridor differential, laryngeal edema association, airway deterioration and escalation/reintubation when significant obstruction is suspected are directly supported.
audit_findings.choice_A: Incorrect; stridor is not specific for laryngospasm and observation alone is unsafe with deterioration.
audit_findings.choice_B: Correct; stabilizes airway/oxygenation while preserving diagnostic uncertainty and escalating appropriately.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; worsening stridor with desaturation is not a routine transfer-ready finding.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: The source item had multiple possible diagnoses; the rewrite removes that ambiguity by testing the universally indicated airway response.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are immediate post-extubation actions; no diagnosis-name cue determines the answer.
audit_findings.blueprint: Direct NCSBN 2026 Reduction of Risk Potential anesthesia-recovery mapping.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked laryngeal edema versus laryngospasm differential, whether reintubation is always required, and treatment overstatement. Final wording says prepare/escalate and reintubate only if significant obstruction is suspected, so no unsupported universal rule remains.
